name: Yusuf Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Yusuf, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sounds good. I'll try to be honest, though I'm usually the guy who sits on the fence until everyone else has jumped.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the personal tax team at Brennan Clarke, a regional firm with three offices, and I'm about a year and a half in. My clients are mostly small landlords, delivery drivers and a few market traders, and my day is chasing them for paperwork, then turning a shoebox of receipts into a tax return. I like the landlords who send everything in one tidy folder, and I dread the ones who send forty photos of crumpled receipts at eleven at night. I'm still slower than I should be on the trickier stuff, like capital gains, so my manager, Helen, reworks a fair bit of what I hand in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's roughly what my dad says will happen. He thinks it's all like the internet bubble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a handy tool and that's all. At work I'd probably make a joke about the partners who spent a fortune on licences. Online I'd share some article about the hype and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it'd mean my job's safe, and I'd be pleased about that. I already use the chatbot now and then to tidy up my chase emails, and that saves me maybe twenty minutes a day. If that's the whole revolution, I can live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and push to get better at capital gains, because that's where Helen keeps catching me out. I'd keep using the chatbot for emails, maybe for checking my maths too, once a few others in the team trust it. And I'd keep overpaying the mortgage on the flat by a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit like when a storm warning turns out to be rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the twenty minutes a day go on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, probably on more returns, because the firm would expect it. But maybe I'd get home before Ana for once. She's a primary teacher and she's always the one cooking because I'm stuck on a client call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at work that already worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The January rush, mainly. Last year I did sixty-hour weeks for a month and made two mistakes my manager had to fix in front of a client. That shook me more than any robot.

say: I'd call AI a **handy tool** and joke about partners overspending on **licences**.
I'd share an article about the **hype** online and leave it there.
think: My job feels **safe**, and the chatbot saves me about **twenty minutes** a day.
My real pressure is the **January rush**, not robots.
do: Keep working as now and study **capital gains**, where my manager catches mistakes.
Keep **overpaying the mortgage** by a hundred a month.
Use the chatbot for emails and **maths checks** once colleagues trust it.
feel: **Calm**, like a storm warning that turns out to be **rain**.
S0.quote: Last year I did sixty-hour weeks for a month and made two mistakes my manager had to fix in front of a client.
fieldNote: His **money** is solid: a flat, savings and a partner with steady **public-sector** pay.
His real stress is the **tax-season** workload and his own errors, not technology.
He adopts AI only **after colleagues** have proven it, true to his steady nature.

steps.text: Study capital gains tax to stop the manager's corrections
Overpay the flat's mortgage by a hundred a month
Use the chatbot to check return maths once the team trusts it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one I can actually picture at Brennan Clarke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the firm owes juniors a training plan, not just a new piece of software. With friends I'd say the profits from this should be taxed and spent on retraining, which, being a tax guy, I'd have numbers for. Online I'd probably share union stuff, which I've never done before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think personal tax returns are the first thing to go. A delivery driver's tax return is a form with numbers in it, and the software can already read the receipts. If the firm needs half the juniors, I'm not sure I'm in the better half yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop being the guy who waits, at least a bit, and get properly good at the AI tools the firm buys, within the first three months. I'd ask Helen to move me towards the advisory side, landlords with messy portfolios, where clients want a person. I'd join the union that's started recruiting at the bigger firms, and I'd build my savings up from eight months to a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because Ana's job is steady and we've got the flat, but I'd feel it every time a senior walked past my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I might need to move teams or firms, and it might mean less money for a bit. She'd tell me to stop catastrophising. Then she'd ask whether teaching needs maths teachers, which she does every time I complain about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop being the guy who waits. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half. I always say I'll jump first and then I wait for Dev, my mate in the audit team, to try it. With this one, though, waiting a year could mean the seat's gone.

say: I'd tell the firm it owes juniors a **training plan**, not just software.
I'd argue the **profits** from AI should be **taxed** and spent on retraining.
think: **Personal tax returns** are among the first things software will take.
If the firm keeps half its juniors, I'm not sure I'm in the **better half**.
do: Master the firm's **AI tools** within the first **three months**.
Ask my manager to move me towards **landlord advisory** work, where clients want a person.
Join the **union** and grow savings from eight months to a **year**.
feel: **Anxious**, though steady household money keeps it from **panic**.
S1.quote: A delivery driver's tax return is a form with numbers in it, and the software can already read the receipts.
fieldNote: He knows his **work type** is first in line and his **skill** is still below average.
His partner's **teaching job** and the flat give real control, which keeps him from alarm.
Interesting tension: he vows to **move first** but admits he waits for a friend.

steps.text: Master the firm's AI tax software in the first three months
Ask the manager for a move to landlord advisory work
Join the union recruiting at larger accounting firms
Build savings from eight months to a full year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd be twenty-nine and basically obsolete. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it loudly: this needs a windfall tax on the AI firms and a basic income, now, not after the damage. I'd go to protests, which I've never done. At work I'd say it in meetings, even with the partners there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone by 2028 and most accounting jobs soon after. Tax work is thinking work from start to finish; there's no hands-on bit for robots to be slow at. The three years before the robots only matter if I can get into some hands-on job fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the mortgage overpayments and keep every spare pound as cash, because cash is what buys time. I'd apply this year for teacher training in maths, since Ana's school is always short, and I'd keep working at Brennan Clarke until they let me go. I'd also join the union and anyone campaigning for an income guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. Like the floor dropped, and I'm meant to be the sensible one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching, if AI can do thinking work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A classroom of thirty eight-year-olds isn't only thinking work, because somebody has to stop them throwing glue. I'm not saying it's safe forever, but it's more about people than spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. We barely use it, and it's two hundred a month with the insurance. And the trip to see my grandparents would become a cheaper trip, which would hurt my mum's feelings more than mine.

say: I'd call for a **windfall tax** on AI firms and a **basic income** now.
I'd join **protests** and raise it in meetings with partners present.
think: My job is likely **gone by 2028**, because tax work is all thinking.
The **robot gap** only helps if I reach **hands-on work** fast.
do: Stop mortgage overpayments and hold **spare cash** instead.
Apply this year for **maths teacher training** near my partner's school.
Sell the **car** to save two hundred a month.
feel: **Frightened**, as if the **floor dropped** while being the sensible one.
S2.quote: A classroom of thirty eight-year-olds isn't only thinking work, because somebody has to stop them throwing glue.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** within two years and loses sleep over it.
He picks **teaching** because it's people-heavy, not because he loves it.
His progressive outlook turns into first-ever **protest** and political action.

steps.text: Stop mortgage overpayments and keep the money as cash
Apply for maths teacher training this year
Join campaigns for a windfall tax and income guarantee
Sell the rarely used car to save two hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a bit of air, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still push for the tax on AI firms and proper retraining money, but I'd frame it as something we can plan, not just a panic. At work I'd push the firm to fund staff who want to retrain, rather than just letting them go in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I get about four more years of accounting, and the honest move is to use them to set up the next thing. I'd be qualified by then, which helps my pay but doesn't change the end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my exams in the next eighteen months, then keep working and saving hard until about 2029. Then I'd do a one-year teacher training course while Ana covers more of the bills, and we'd pay it back to each other later. I'd use the AI tools daily at work until then, since being good with them keeps me employed longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but five years of warning turns losing my job into a project rather than a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousin who's thinking about accountancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Mateo not to bother with an accounting degree. Do something with people, or a trade, and learn to use the AI on the side. That would be a strange thing for me to say, given I loved my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ana would cover more bills. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not brilliantly, if I'm honest. My dad always paid for everything and I don't believe in that, but it still stings a bit. We'd write it down, like a little loan, so it feels fair.

say: I'd push for an **AI tax** and retraining money, framed as **planning**.
I'd ask the firm to **fund retraining** rather than lay staff off in 2031.
think: I get about **four more years** of accounting before it ends.
Qualifying lifts my **pay** but doesn't change the **end point**.
do: Finish my **professional exams** within eighteen months.
Use the firm's **AI tools daily** to stay useful until **2029**.
Take a one-year **teacher training** course with my partner covering more bills.
feel: Still **worried**, but it feels like a **project** rather than a fire.
S3.quote: Five years of warning turns losing my job into a project rather than a fire.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **plan a switch**, though he still expects accounting to end.
He would advise his **cousin** against the degree he loved.
Leaning on his **partner** financially stings, despite his progressive views.

steps.text: Finish the professional exams within eighteen months
Use the AI tax tools every day at work until 2029
Save hard so a year of teacher training is covered
Push the firm and union to fund staff retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a career, really. A short one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we have no excuse for chaos. I'd say it at work: let's plan, let's train people, let's make sure the gains get shared. Online I'd be the boring guy posting about tax policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years means I could make senior, earn well, maybe pay off the flat, and then step off before the end. I'd feel lucky compared with people in two years. But I'd still be thirty-seven and starting again, and that's not small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify and stick with Brennan Clarke for now, using the AI tools more as they prove themselves. I'd put the extra pay into clearing the mortgage by about 2032. Around then I'd look at teaching or something with people, and in the meantime I'd stay in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. It's far enough off that I can almost pretend, which is probably the dangerous part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can almost pretend. What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana, probably. She'd keep asking about the plan. And Helen retiring around 2030 would be a wake-up call, because her job would go to software, not to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still have kids, probably around thirty. But whatever happens to my job, I want the flat paid off first, so the roof is ours.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for chaos, and gains must be **shared**.
I'd be the person posting about **tax policy** online.
think: I could make **senior**, pay off the flat, then **step off** before the end.
Starting again at **thirty-seven** is still a big deal.
do: Qualify and use **AI tools** more as they prove themselves.
Clear the **mortgage** by about **2032** with the extra pay.
Look at **teaching** around 2032 and stay in the union.
feel: **Uneasy** more than scared, and aware that pretending is **dangerous**.
S4.quote: Whatever happens to my job, I want the flat paid off first, so the roof is ours.
fieldNote: Ten years still ends his **job**; he just gets time to **pay off** the flat first.
He fears **complacency** more than shock, and relies on his partner to keep him honest.
He expects his manager's **senior role** to go to software, not to him.

steps.text: Adopt the AI tax tools as each one proves itself
Pay off the flat's mortgage by about 2032
Have children around thirty, once the flat is paid off

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. With two years, I'd be competing with every other junior accountant for a teaching course or anything else. What would help is a windfall tax on the AI firms paying for retraining, plus a basic income while people retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who it's fair to blame. People say us juniors should have learned faster. Nobody hired me to compete with a machine, so the firms that profit from it should carry some of the cost.

headlineQuote: Nobody hired me to compete with a machine, so the firms that profit from it should carry some of the cost.
portrait: Yusuf is a **junior tax accountant** at a regional firm, preparing returns for landlords, drivers and traders.
He owns a **small flat**, has eight months saved, and lives with Ana, a **primary teacher**.
He uses AI **now and then**, usually after a colleague tries it first.
He moves from calm to **alarmed**, blaming firms profiting from AI and calling for a **windfall tax**.
His fallback plan is **maths teaching**, chosen because classrooms are about people.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, since every junior would be **competing** for the same few exits.
whatWouldHelp: A **windfall tax** on AI firms funding retraining, plus a **basic income** while people study.
